reason: The provided sources fully support a surprising 45-second story with at least 10 multiply-sourced claims.
story: On May 22, 1915, two signalmen changing shifts late at Quintinshill box in Scotland hid a local passenger train on the main southbound line. Distracted by a newspaper and paperwork, they forgot it was there. Minutes later, a troop train carrying 500 soldiers from the Royal Scots to Gallipoli slammed into the stationary local service at full speed. Before survivors could escape, a northbound express train ploughed into the wreckage. Obsolete wooden carriages equipped with gas lighting ruptured, igniting a horrific inferno that burned for nearly a day. Over 200 people died, making it Britain's deadliest rail disaster.
angle: Two signalmen hid a passenger train on the main line during a late shift change, forgot about it entirely, and allowed a troop train to thunder straight into it at 80 miles per hour.

claims.claim: The Quintinshill rail disaster occurred on 22 May 1915.

evidence.quote: The Quintinshill rail disaster was a multi-train rail crash which occurred on 22 May 1915 outside the Quintinshill signal box near Gretna Green in Dumfriesshire, Scotland.
The Quintinshill Rail disaster occurred on the 22nd of May, 1915 near Gretna Green in Dumfriesshire.

claims.claim: It remains the worst rail disaster in British history.

evidence.quote: It resulted in the deaths of over 200 people and remains the worst rail disaster in British history.
It remains the worst UK rail crash in terms of loss of life.

claims.claim: The crash involved a troop train colliding with a stationary local passenger train.

evidence.quote: The first collision occurred when a southbound troop train travelling from Larbert to Liverpool collided with the stationary local train.
Five trains were involved: a troop train collided with a stationary local train and the disaster was compounded when, moments later, a northbound express train thundered into the wreckage

claims.claim: A northbound express train struck the wreckage a minute later.

evidence.quote: A minute later the wreckage was struck by a northbound sleeping car express train travelling from London Euston to Glasgow Central.
Barely 30 seconds after the initial impact, an express train travelling in the opposite direction ploughed into the mass of wreckage at nearly 50mph.

claims.claim: Gas from the lighting system ignited, starting a massive fire.

evidence.quote: Gas from the Pintsch gas lighting system of the old wooden carriages of the troop train ignited, starting a fire which soon engulfed all five trains.
The gas tanks on the troop train ruptured, causing a fire so hot it buckled the steel carriages of the express.

claims.claim: The soldiers on the troop train were primarily from the 1/7th Battalion of the Royal Scots heading for Gallipoli.

evidence.quote: Those killed were mainly Territorial soldiers from the 1/7th (Leith) Battalion, the Royal Scots heading for Gallipoli.

The 7th Royal Scots – who were travelling aboard the troop train – accounted for 216 of those killed. The battalion had been en-route from Larbert to Liverpool, and then on to join the conflict at Gallipoli.

claims.claim: The official death toll was over 200 people (around 226 to 227).

evidence.quote: The official death toll was 227 (215 soldiers, nine other passengers and three railway employees)
Estimates of the dead are put at around 230, with 246 injured.

claims.claim: The disaster was caused by the neglect of rules by two signalmen, George Meakin and James Tinsley.

evidence.quote: An official inquiry, completed on 17 June 1915 for the Board of Trade, found the cause of the collision to be neglect of the rules by two signalmen.

After a series of investigations, including a fatal accident inquiry and a coroner’s inquest, the negligence of two local signalmen, James Tinsley and George Meakin was held to blame for the disaster.

claims.claim: The signalmen had shunted the northbound local train onto the southbound main line and then forgot about it.

evidence.quote: With the northbound loop occupied, the northbound local train had been reversed onto the southbound line to allow passage of two late-running northbound sleepers. Its presence was then overlooked, and the southbound troop train was cleared for passage.
a couple of signalmen simply forgot they had left a train standing on the main line.

claims.claim: The fire burned until the morning of the next day.

evidence.quote: the fire was not extinguished until the morning of the next day, despite the best efforts of railway staff and the Carlisle fire brigade.
It was not until the following day that the blaze was fully put out.

claims.claim: Peter Stoddart was among the survivors of the troop train.

evidence.quote: The last known survivor of the accident, Peter Stoddart, was interviewed near Wisbech by Michael Simkins in around 1985.
"Dear Sir, I am a survivor of the train smash at Quintinshill and am willing to assist you in any way I can. Yours faithfully: Peter Stoddart."

disputed: Whether the signalman James Tinsley suffered from epilepsy which contributed to his forgetfulness (noted in police/Crown records and modern documentaries, but not standard in the Board of Trade inquiry report; attribute or leave out)

Allegations of mercy killings or officers shooting trapped men in the fire (mentioned in survivor recollections and press reports, but never formally documented or officially recorded; attribute as 'according to some accounts')
The precise final casualty numbers, which vary slightly between sources (e.g., 227 official vs. 230 estimated; use approximate terms)
